clue.text: It might be the story of a French bed takes time, when the true ending is uncertain.

parts.note: lit is the French word for a bed
an era is a period of time

indicators.note: an uncertain ending is an unsettled outcome, so the letters of the word true are jumbled

explanation.surface: A tale about a French bed takes ages to tell, and nobody is sure how it really ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ending is uncertain' turns TRUE into TURE, which also closes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A story is one example of written work, so literature covers it.

clue.text: If you glare at somebody, you might get one, as you may have read.

definitions.text: If you glare at somebody, you might get one, as you may have read.

parts.words: If you glare at somebody, you might get one, as you may have read
parts.note: glare at someone and they may return the furious stare; it is also the title of John Osborne's 1956 play, something you may have read

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase describes the reply to a glare and is also the title of John Osborne's 1956 play.
explanation.definitionFit: John Osborne's famous play about the 'angry young man' Jimmy Porter carries this title.

clue.text: The things here given to you and me helped the Argonauts.

parts.note: these refers to things close at hand
you and me together are us

explanation.surface: Some items handed to the two of us were of use to Jason's crew.
explanation.walkthrough: In some versions of the myth the Athenian hero sailed with Jason among the crew of the Argo.
explanation.definitionFit: Theseus is listed among the heroes who sailed on the Argo, so he is one who helped that crew.

clue.text: Not necessarily confined to Spanish plain song.

definitions.text: Not necessarily confined to Spanish plain song.

parts.words: Not necessarily confined to Spanish plain song
parts.note: the My Fair Lady song claims the Spanish weather stays mainly on the plain, so some of it need not land there

explanation.walkthrough: 'The Rain in Spain' from My Fair Lady says it 'stays mainly in the plain' (often recalled as 'falls mainly'), so not all of it stays there; 'plain song' also suggests plainsong, church chant.
explanation.definitionFit: Rainfall is the precipitation that comes down from clouds, which the song locates mostly on the Spanish plain.

clue.text: You might find it sort of dry and hot with one in your larynx.

indicators.note: a sort of something is a variant of it, so the letters of these words are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Something you might feel in a parched, burning throat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges DRY, HOT and I; the answer is found at the larynx because its main cartilage, the Adam's apple, is part of the larynx.
explanation.definitionFit: The thyroid cartilage is the largest cartilage of the voice box, so it sits in the throat's larynx.

clue.text: Gives up again and goes back?

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read as RE- plus CEDES: hands over once more

explanation.walkthrough: To cede is to give up, so splitting the answer as RE-CEDES gives the first sense; the question mark flags this split.
explanation.definitionFit: Floodwaters or a hairline that withdraw are said to retreat, and that is the second sense.

clue.text: Is it fair to build up a picture of such a slightly incredulous opening?

parts.note: something fair or right is just
to imagine is to build up a picture in the mind

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about whether it is right to piece together an image of some doubtful start.
explanation.walkthrough: The two halves of the phrase are clued one after the other, and the whole phrase is what a mildly disbelieving speaker might begin with.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'just imagine!' is a common exclamation that begins a remark of mild astonishment or disbelief.

clue.text: It's not even what the most jejune quality displays.

indicators.note: to display is to put on show, so the answer is on view within the run of letters

parts.note: the letters run across these two words

explanation.surface: Some feature that a very naive trait shows off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'displays' says the answer is on show inside 'jejune quality'; jejune means naive or dull, a word chosen for the letters it supplies.
explanation.definitionFit: Two things that are not even or level are unequal in size or amount.

clue.text: What one hopes to hear after the oil spill has been accounted for?

definitions.text: What one hopes to hear after the oil spill has been accounted for?

parts.words: What one hopes to hear after the oil spill has been accounted for
parts.note: after a spill, everyone wants the shoreline to be clean again; the phrase is also the signal that it is safe to go ahead

explanation.walkthrough: The everyday phrase means it is safe to proceed; read literally it means the shoreline is clean, just what is wanted after an oil spill.
explanation.definitionFit: The expression is the all-clear given when no danger remains, here applied literally to the polluted shoreline.

clue.text: Stage money? (It goes to show you what might happen next, as they say.)

definitions.text: It goes to show you what might happen next, as they say.

parts.note: a stage play is drama
bills are paper money, in American usage banknotes

explanation.surface: Fake banknotes used in a theatre production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stage money' suggests props, but stage gives PLAY and money gives BILLS; 'it goes to show' puns on show as a theatre performance.
explanation.definitionFit: A playbill is a poster or programme advertising a forthcoming theatre performance, telling you what is coming.

clue.text: It probably isn't good for you, but so be it, as you will! It's on your head!

definitions.text: It probably isn't good for you

indicators.note: in whatever order you like, so the letters of so be it and the extra letter may be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of your

explanation.surface: A shrug of resignation about something unhealthy, with the blame landing on the listener.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's on your head!' sounds like a warning about blame, but it puts the first letter of 'your' with SO BE IT, and 'as you will' mixes the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Being very overweight is a well-known health risk, so it is hardly good for anyone.

clue.text: A body of colleagues might be one.

definitions.text: A body of colleagues might be one.

parts.words: A body of colleagues might be one
parts.note: an organised group of fellow professionals is called by this name

explanation.walkthrough: The word 'colleagues' and the answer share a Latin root meaning chosen together, which is the clue's quiet joke.
explanation.definitionFit: An organised society of people with a shared profession, such as an electoral or medical body, is called by this name.

clue.text: Raised loaf, by the sound of it.

indicators.note: says the answer is spelt as heard, a word pronounced the same as the baked food

parts.note: a loaf is a portion of bread

explanation.surface: A loaf that has risen in the oven, judging from how it sounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by the sound of it' says to take a word that is pronounced like BREAD. 'Raised' looks like it describes bread rising, but it is the definition, as in children raised by parents.
explanation.definitionFit: Children brought up by their parents are said to have been reared, or raised.

clue.text: It seems the question of your fabrication has no end of polite acknowledgment.

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read literally: asking in what way you make something
second meaning: the formal greeting said on being introduced

explanation.walkthrough: Read literally the greeting asks how you do (make) things, which is what 'your fabrication' means; 'has no end of' just links the two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a formal greeting exchanged when two people are introduced, a courteous acknowledgment.

clue.text: Reputedly heavenly products.

parts.note: the saying claims that these unions are made in heaven

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb says such unions are made in heaven, so they are 'products' of heaven by repute.
explanation.definitionFit: Weddings or unions of couples are proverbially made in heaven, hence 'reputedly heavenly products'.

clue.text: A basis for rumination about the main part, as a matter of course.

indicators.note: one word placed around another, so the chewed food goes about the lead role

parts.note: cud is the food a cow chews over again when ruminating
the star plays the main part in a show

explanation.surface: Chewing things over, roughly the central point, as a matter of routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' means the chewed food goes around the lead role. 'as a matter of course' sounds like 'routinely', but a course here is a stage of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Custard is a sweet sauce eaten with the pudding stage of a meal, so it is matter served at one course.

clue.text: Best, if less apparent, but chokes things off inside.

indicators.note: apparent means visible, so the answer can be seen sitting in the run of clue words

parts.note: the letters run on across these three words

explanation.surface: It is best when less obvious, though it bottles things up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'if less apparent' reads like a comment on being best, but 'apparent' is what tells you the word is visible inside 'Best, if less'.
explanation.definitionFit: To smother or suppress something, such as a yawn or feelings, is to hold it in by choking it off.

clue.text: Showing excellent shape about the point, meanwhile.

indicators.note: the phrase for good shape goes around the compass point

parts.note: in trim means in good condition
E, east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A runner looking fit around a certain time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps IN TRIM around E, the compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: An interim arrangement is one for the time in between, so the word means for now or meanwhile.

clue.text: Showing less than 10, but it might make the coat less heavy.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: slimmer, with a lower count or weight, as in less than ten stone

definitions.text: it might make the coat less heavy
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a solvent added to paint to make the coat less thick

explanation.walkthrough: 'coat' looks like clothing, but here it is a coat of paint, and a solvent thins it.
explanation.definitionFit: Paint thinner is a solvent such as turpentine used to dilute paint, giving a lighter application.

clue.text: Some people carry it as a sort of protection, like a silencer.

definitions.text: Some people carry it as a sort of protection
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a scarf worn around the neck against the cold
second meaning: the device on a car exhaust or gun that deadens noise

explanation.walkthrough: 'carry it as protection' suggests a weapon, especially beside 'silencer', but the first sense is a warm scarf.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a warm scarf and, in American usage, the noise-reducing part of a car exhaust.

clue.text: Was he famous for shaping an underground political unit in one?

parts.note: a cell is a small secret group within a political movement
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Asks whether some revolutionary is famous for setting up a secret cell.
explanation.walkthrough: Benvenuto Cellini was a Renaissance Italian goldsmith and sculptor, famous for shaping metal; 'shaping' looks like organising the cell.
explanation.definitionFit: Cellini was the celebrated Florentine goldsmith and sculptor of the sixteenth century, known for his metalwork and his memoirs.

clue.text: Hearty type that makes jokes with the CIA organization?

parts.note: a card is a comedian, someone who is always joking

indicators.note: organising letters means putting them in a new order, so the letters of CIA are rearranged

explanation.surface: A jovial joker who works with the American spy agency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organization' looks like it describes the CIA, but it signals a rearrangement of CIA as IAC. 'Hearty' is read literally: of the heart.
explanation.definitionFit: Cardiac means relating to the heart, the literal sense of hearty here.

clue.text: Would you find it in any circumstances after getting in? Nonsense!

indicators.note: the second part follows the first, so the wrapped word comes after the short word

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the word in tells you one piece sits within another, so the pronoun goes into the word any

explanation.surface: A doubtful question about whether something could be found anywhere once you got inside.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'in' is the container signal, making ANITY, and 'after getting' sets that behind the second 'in', taken as written; 'circumstances' is surface padding.
explanation.definitionFit: Inanity is silliness or senselessness, the quality of talk that is nonsense.

clue.text: Orwellian breeding place?

parts.note: a place where livestock are bred, as described in the George Orwell novel of that title

explanation.walkthrough: A farm is where animals are bred; the George Orwell book's title names such a place.
explanation.definitionFit: Orwell's 1945 satire takes its title from the livestock holding the animals take over.

clue.text: Capital C (not the pica sort) representing mineral.

indicators.note: not means leave out, so the stated letters are taken away

parts.note: taken as written; the answer showing at the end of these words is a coincidence of the removal, not a separate hidden word
a sort of pica is its letters reordered; pica is also a printer's type size, which fits the capital-letter surface

explanation.surface: A printing note about a large letter in some type size stands for a mineral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the pica sort' is CAPI, the letters of PICA rearranged, and 'not' removes them from CAPITALC, leaving the mineral; 'representing' just links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Talc is a soft mineral, magnesium silicate, ground to make talcum powder.

clue.text: See 3
An uncouth man, the slippery type, but still stylish.

parts.note: gent is short for gentleman, a man
an eel is a proverbially slippery fish

explanation.surface: A boorish, shifty fellow who nonetheless dresses well.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'uncouth' man is a joke: a gent should be anything but uncouth, yet he still yields the refined answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Genteel means refined and polite, with a fashionable elegance of manner.

clue.text: See 6
The opposite might be often done.

definitions.text: The opposite might be often done.

parts.words: The opposite might be often done
parts.note: the opposite of often is seldom, and the opposite of well done meat is underdone; the answer covers both

explanation.walkthrough: Both senses hide in 'often done': the reverse of often, and the reverse of meat that is well done.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means seldom found, and also lightly cooked steak, the opposite of well done.

clue.text: One might set a course for your home.

definitions.text: One might set a course for your home.

parts.words: One might set a course for your home
parts.note: a course is a single row of bricks laid in a wall, not a route plotted for a journey

explanation.walkthrough: 'set a course' sounds like navigating towards your house, but a course is a layer of bricks in its walls.
explanation.definitionFit: A builder who lays bricks puts them down in rows called courses when building a house.
